{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=preference+formation+path+dependence+longitudinal+behavior+active+learning&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"title\": [\"Public Transit Path Choice Modeling with Behavior Driven Preference Learning: An Interpretable Framework\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Public transit path choice behavior modeling is fundamental to travel demand analysis and transit guidance strategies. Discrete choice models based on Multinomial Logit remain the dominant approach for path choice analysis, yet predictive accuracy is frequently constrained by underlying assumptions; conversely, the few exiting deep learning-based methods suffer from weak interpretability. More importantly, neither method effectively captures individual preferences, making it difficult to reflect traveler heterogeneity. To address these limitations, a behavior-driven preference learning-based public transit path choice model is proposed in this study. First, individual behavioral features are constructed using historical data, and a preference mining layer is designed to learn latent preference representations from long-term historical behaviors. Then, gating mechanisms and attention mechanisms are introduced to achieve differentiated attention to path features among different travelers. Furthermore, a comprehensive model interpretation framework is developed by leveraging methods such as Accumulated Local Effects, Integrated Gradients, and Adaptive Clustering. Finally, empirical studies are conducted based on real-world data from Beijing, and comparative analyses with existing methods are performed. Performance analysis results indicate that an accuracy rate of 83.90% is achieved by the proposed model, representing a improvement of 11.86 percentage points. Furthermore, it is demonstrated through interpretability analyses that complex nonlinear relationships among intricate path features, contextual features, and individual preferences can be more effectively captured. Additionally, the distinctly different decision-making logics exhibited by various preference groups during the path choice process are reasonably explained.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"published\": {\"…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+reasoning+self+correction+falsification+limitations+oversight&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"title\": [\"Automated Oversight Diagnostic Self-Correction and Failure-Aware Reasoning for GUI Agents(ChinaMM)\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid evolution of Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) has significantly advanced autonomous GUI agents. However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. We will publicly release our code.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8\", \"title\": [\"What Are the Limitations of the Situation Calculus?\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1991]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/cbo9780511576430.008\", \…

Eric J. Horvitz

Stanford University
Stanford, California 94305
John S. Breese
Rockwell International Science Center
Palo Alto Laboratory
444 High Street
Palo Alto, CA 94301
January 1990
Technical Report KSL-90-26, Knowledge Systems Laboratory, Stanford University.
Abstract
We can achieve signiﬁcant gains in the value of computation by metareasoning about the nature
or extent of base-level problem solving before executing a solution. However, resources that are
irrevocably committed to metareasoning are not available for executing a solution. Thus, it is
important to determine the portion of resources we wish to apply to metareasoning and control
versus to the execution of a solution plan. Recent research on rational agency has highlighted
the importance of limiting the consumption of resources by metareasoning machinery. We
shall introduce the metareasoning-partitionproblem—the problem of ideally apportioning costly
reasoning resources to planning a solution versus applying resource to executing a solution to
a problem. We exercise prototypical metareasoning-partition models to probe the relationships
between time allocated to metareasoning and to execution for diﬀerent problem classes. Finally,
we examine the value of metareasoning in the context of our functional analyses.

dation under Grant IRI-8703710, and by the U.S. Army Research Oﬃce under Grant P-25514-EL. Computing
facilities were provided by the SUMEX-AIM Resource under NLM Grant LM05208.
